name: AssangeDAO purchase of Clock (2022)
why: Covered by pak--clock (onchain-pak batch). Extra facts to merge there: 17,422 ETH raised via Juicebox, $JUSTICE token at 1 ETH = 1,000,000, above ConstitutionDAO's 11,613 ETH; video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7AzW59oWfKA (Epicenter podcast with Gabriel Shipton).

name: PleasrDAO
why: Collector DAO that buys culturally significant NFTs; members vote, but no artist authored its rules.

name: ConstitutionDAO (2021)
why: Crowd DAO that tried to buy a copy of the US Constitution; a platform with no artistic author.

name: Fingerprints DAO
why: Collector DAO for smart-contract art (commissioned terra0's Seed Capital); no artist-authored rules.

name: Flamingo DAO
why: Investment/collector DAO for NFTs; no artistic author.

name: Friends With Benefits (FWB)
why: Token-gated social DAO for creatives; no single authored artwork protocol.

name: Andy Ayrey, Infinite Backrooms (2024)
why: Two Claude-3-Opus instances conversing thousands of times; machine-only process, no group behaviour.

name: Jonas Lund, The Fear Of Missing Out (2013)
why: Software tells the artist what to make; the rules address the artist alone, not a group.

name: Jonas Lund, New Now (2016)
why: Neural network trained on his own work dictates new pieces; no group behaviour.

name: Jonas Lund, JLT Futures (2024)
why: Forward contracts on future Jonas Lund artworks appraised by the JLT board; covered inside the Jonas Lund Token entry.

name: Plantoid Garden at Burning Man 2018
why: Three large Plantoids shown at Burning Man 2018; covered inside the Plantoid entry.

name: The Tree That Owns Itself (Athens, Georgia)
why: Legendary 19th-century deed giving a tree ownership of itself; folk precedent with no artistic author.

name: Kei Kreutler, talks 'Mediums of Memory' and 'Autonomous ecologies at a distance'
why: Talks and essays on DAOs (her essay is in the theory batch); no artwork with a group protocol found.

name: Stelarc — Ping Body (1996)
why: Muscles actuated by internet ping times; the body is moved by network data, not by participants acting under a rule.

name: Andrew Badr — Your World of Text (2009)
why: Infinite shared text grid anyone can type on; needs a verifiable image.

name: Ze Frank — Earth Sandwich (2006)
why: Challenge from the show with zefrank to place two slices of bread at antipodes simultaneously; realised by viewers in Spain and New Zealand.

name: Paul Sermon — Telematic Dreaming (1992)
why: Two remote participants share a projected bed; intimate telepresence rather than a crowd protocol.

name: pxls.space and other r/place clones
why: Fan-run canvases copying the r/place rule without a distinct author or artistic intent.

name: Constant Dullaart — High Retention, Slow Delivery (2014)
why: Bought 2.5 million fake Instagram followers and gave art-world accounts 100,000 each; the 'crowd' is purchased bot accounts, so no participants act under the rule.

name: Lauren Lee McCarthy — Follower (2016)
why: One-to-one performance in which the artist follows a single user for a day; no group acts under the rule.

name: Lauren Lee McCarthy — LAUREN (2017)
why: The artist herself acts as a human Alexa for one household at a time; not a crowd protocol (its crowd version is SOMEONE).

name: Lauren Lee McCarthy — Crowdpilot (2014)
why: App letting strangers listen to a conversation and advise the user in real time; project page currently empty.

name: Josh Wardle — Wordle (2021)
why: Single-player daily word game; the shared puzzle creates a social ritual but players do not act together under a rule.

name: Eva & Franco Mattes — Emily's Video (2012), No Fun (2010), The Bots (2020)
why: Reaction videos of respondents, a staged suicide on Chatroulette, and actors reenacting moderators; people are recorded rather than acting under a published rule.

name: Neal Agarwal — Infinite Craft and other web toys
why: Mostly single-player browser games; shared 'first discoveries' are a side effect, not a collective rule.

name: Google Creative Lab — Quick, Draw! (2016)
why: Drawing game that collects doodles into a dataset for machine learning; a corporate data product rather than an authored crowd work.

name: Aaron Koblin — Flight Patterns (2005), New York Talk Exchange (2008)
why: Visualisations of aircraft and telecom data; no participants acting under a rule.

name: Harm van den Dorpel – Death Imitates Language (2016)
why: Checked: selection and breeding are done by the artist through 'likes' (plus visitor statistics), not by collectors; fails test 3 as an on-chain co-authored work.

name: mfers (sartoshi, 2021)
why: CC0 stick-figure PFP collection with heavy derivative culture; sartoshi later left the project to the community. No authored rule beyond the CC0 licence shapes collective behaviour; revisit only if the hand-over is documented as a protocol.

name: Loot Survivor (Provable Games, 2023)
why: On-chain roguelike built on Loot on Starknet; a commercial game rather than an artist-authored protocol.

name: CryptoKitties (Axiom Zen / Dapper Labs, 2017)
why: Collectors breed cats on-chain; a commercial game, useful only as context for breeding mechanics.

name: Archillect (Pak, 2014)
why: AI image curator whose picks respond to audience engagement; followers give feedback but do not act under an authored rule, so it fails test 2–3.

name: The Switch (Pak, 2021)
why: 1/1 whose owner can call a function once to change it; a single-owner mechanic, not collective behaviour.

name: Hate (Pak, 2022)
why: Tokens issued to critics and later moved to a burn address by Pak; the rule acts on individuals, not a group.

name: The Title (Pak, 2021)
why: Identical NFTs sold under different titles and pricing; a comment on framing without collective rules.

name: Pak open editions on Nifty Gateway (Project X, 2020)
why: Early time-limited open editions credited to Pak; context for The Fungible and Merge rather than a separate protocol work.

name: Checks Elements (Jack Butcher, 2023)
why: Monoprints paired with tokens; no collector mechanism.

name: Gas Wars (Jack Butcher, 2025)
why: Art Blocks release where price follows token number in a 500-second window; a mint mechanic, collective behaviour only predicted.

name: Wrappers (Jack Butcher, 2026)
why: 80 images distributed by blind draw; holders have no rule to act on.

name: Mad Dog Jones, REPLICATOR (2021)
why: A 1/1 that generates new editions over time; reproduction without a group rule.

name: Burnt Banksy (2021)
why: A bought Banksy print burned and minted as an NFT by a company; no artist-authored protocol.

name: EtherRock (2017)
why: 100 rocks with a rising mint price and in-contract market, but the author is anonymous, so it fails the authored-protocol test.

name: Kevin Abosch, Yellow Lambo (2018)
why: Neon sculpture of a token address sold to one buyer; no collective rule.

name: Mitchell F. Chan, Digital Zones of Immaterial Pictorial Sensibility (2017)
why: Already in onchain-pak (ritual burn destroys ETH from the artist's contract).

name: Rhea Myers, Certificate of Inauthenticity (2020)
why: NFT certificates growing out of the DECAL gold castings of Shareable Readymades; covered inside that entry.

name: Rhea Myers, Tokens Equal Text (2019)
why: ERC-998 composable tokens whose IDs read as text; no collective rule.

name: Tino Sehgal
why: Constructed situations (This Progress, These associations) performed by trained 'interpreters' under verbal rules; no photos allowed.

name: Morton Feldman: Intersection 3 (1953)
why: Graph score for one pianist; Getty Scores Project chapter 1; performer freedom but no group.

name: Sylvano Bussotti: Five Piano Pieces for David Tudor (1959)
why: Graphic score for a single performer; Getty chapter 3; no group carries out the rules.

name: Robert Filliou, Principle of Equivalence (well made, badly made, not made)
why: Artist-made object series; no rule for a group.

name: Francis Alÿs, Children's Games (1999–)
why: Films existing children's games; the rules are not authored by the artist.

name: Ai Weiwei, Sunflower Seeds (2010)
why: Made by about 1,600 artisans as fabrication labour; no rule shapes a group's behaviour as the work.

name: Lygia Clark, Estruturação do Self (Structuring of the Self, 1976–1988)
why: One-to-one therapeutic sessions with relational objects; not addressed to a group.

name: Christo and Jeanne-Claude, large installations
why: Large paid crews install a design; crowd behaviour is not the work.

name: Wikipedia article 'Protocolar Art'
why: Flagged on Wikipedia as possibly AI-generated (March 2026); promotes a single theorist's term. Not a reliable source.

name: terra0 whitepaper (Paul Seidler et al., 2016)
why: Owned by the autonomous batch together with the terra0 work.

name: Yoko Ono, Grapefruit (1964)
why: Belongs to the score batch.
